results.title: State of the GPU Rental Market, October 2026 | FastGPU
highlights:
In the week to October 10, NVIDIA's Blackwell GPUs and the H200 were the hardest to rent on demand. The providers that publish stock information had a B300 rentable in 75% of their stock checks, a B200 in 76% and an H200 in 76%, while 15 of the 24 GPUs with enough signal to measure were rentable in every check. Over the same days, the cheapest posted B200 did not move at all: it stood at $3.69/hr in each of the last 7 daily fixings, set by the same provider every day, while the typical provider's price rose. The GPU rental market in October 2026 behaves like two markets: a tight one for Blackwell and H200, priced in a narrow band and getting dearer, and a loose one for older cards that are always in stock, priced far apart and noisy at the floor.

...

Every figure is a snapshot as of October 11, 2026, and every figure is a link. Live prices are as of 4:04 PM UTC that day, availability covers completed UTC days through October 10, and the daily fixings are the ones frozen at 07:00 UTC on October 11. Click any number to reach the page or API row behind it, which shows the current value; where a link and this report disagree, the link is current and the report is dated.

...

- Blackwell and H200 are scarce on demand. In the week to October 10, the B300 was rentable in 75% of stock checks, the B200 in 76%, the H200 in 76%, and the RTX PRO 6000 in 79%, while 15 GPUs were rentable in 100% of checks.
- The H100 SXM had the week's biggest drop. Its rentable share fell from 100% to 87% week on week (it was back at 100% on October 10), and all 8 of its confirmed list-price changes in the last 60 days were rises.
- The floor holds while list prices climb. The price index stands at 99.1, 0.9% below its August base, yet the price-change log holds 81 rises against 4 cuts. The B300's median rose from $8.50 to $9.51 in a week while its floor did not move.
- Rent runs far above the chip's book cost. An H100 SXM rents for a median $3.95/hr; written off over CoreWeave's 6-year schedule, the chip costs $0.48 per GPU-hour and pays for itself in 8.7 months rented around the clock.
- The best GPU per dollar depends on which price you use. At each GPU's floor, the MI355X buys the most benchmarked throughput per rented dollar in one MLPerf® Inference v6.1 scenario, 5,343 tokens/s per $/hr (derived, unverified); at the median price, the B200, B300, GB200 and MI300X are close to a tie.

...

Two of FastGPU's price series point in opposite directions this autumn. The GPU Cloud Price Index, a Jevons index of the cheapest rentable price for each tracked GPU, stands at 99.1: 0.9% below its base of August 13, with 8 of 18 tracked GPUs cheaper, 7 pricier and 3 flat. By that measure GPU rental prices have gone sideways, as our September report on whether GPU cloud prices are falling found with less data.

The price-change log, which records confirmed moves in providers' own posted rates and leaves out marketplace hosts, tells a different story. Of its 85 entries, 81 are rises and 4 are cuts. In the 60-day window to October 10, every confirmed list-price change for the four flagship data-center GPUs was a rise: 8 for the H100 SXM across 5 providers, with a median step of 14.3%; 6 for the H200 (median step 17.5%); 7 for the B200 ( 17.7%, or $1.20 per GPU-hour); and 6 for the B300 ( 10.4%). One recorded example: RunPod's on-demand B200 went from $6.79 to $7.99 per GPU-hour on October 8. FastGPU's monthly State of GPU prices for September counted 15 posted prices that rose and 0 that fell.

The two series reconcile once you look at who sets the floor, which the daily fixings record each day at 07:00 UTC. For the H100 SXM it was a Vast.ai host on 7 of 7 fixing days, and the same holds for the A100 80GB, L40S and RTX PRO 6000. For the B200 and B300 it was DeepInfra on 7 of 7 days, and for the H200, DeepInfra on 4 of 7. Marketplace hosts reprice constantly and are not list prices; the B200 and B300 floors have not changed once in 67 recorded one-day changes since August 4. Neither kind of seller responds to the list-price rises at the specialized GPU clouds, so the floor, and an index built on floors, stays flat while the price a typical buyer meets climbs.

The medians show that climb directly. Between the fixings of October 5 and October 11, the B300's on-demand median across 10 providers outside the hyperscalers rose from $8.50 to $9.51 per GPU-hour ($9.51 / $8.50 = 1.119, a rise of about 12%), and the B200's from $6.89 to $7.13, while both floors stayed exactly where they were. The H100 SXM median held at $3.95. A week of fixings is a short record and nothing here is a forecast, but the budgeting lesson is plain: a floor that does not move is not evidence that prices are stable. Budget from the median, and check the price-change log for the providers you use.

...

| GPU | Floor volatility, 30 days | Spread, P90 / P10 | Floor set by | List-price changes, 60 days (rises / cuts) |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| B200 | 0.0% a day | 1.68x | DeepInfra, 7 of 7 days | 7 / 0 |
| B300 | 0.0% a day | 1.69x | DeepInfra, 7 of 7 days | 6 / 0 |
| H200 | 13.2% a day | 1.81x | DeepInfra, 4 of 7 days | 6 / 0 |
| RTX PRO 6000 | 6.3% a day | 2.00x | Vast.ai, 7 of 7 days | 8 / 1 |
| H100 SXM | 9.6% a day | 2.55x | Vast.ai, 7 of 7 days | 8 / 0 |
| L40S | 13.9% a day | 2.85x | Vast.ai, 7 of 7 days | 5 / 0 |
| A100 80GB | 28.9% a day | 3.53x | Vast.ai, 7 of 7 days | 5 / 1 |

Floor volatility mostly measures who sets the floor. Where a fixed-price seller holds it, as DeepInfra does for the B200 and B300, it is zero. Where a marketplace host holds it, the floor jumps whenever that host's machine is rented or withdrawn. The H100 SXM shows the pattern: its largest one-day move in the window was +35.4%, from $1.32 to $1.79 on September 11; from September 10 to October 5 the floor ran up 41.5% to $1.87, then fell 20.8% to $1.48 by October 7. The record starts on August 4, so each GPU has at most 67 one-day changes: read these figures as a comparison between GPUs with wide error bars, not as a risk model.

Spread runs the other way from scarcity. The GPUs that are hardest to rent are priced in the tightest band: the B200's 90th-percentile provider charges $8.59 and its 10th-percentile provider $5.10, across 12 providers. For the A100 80GB the same ratio is 3.53x ( $3.52 against $1.00 across 15 providers). Provider choice is worth more the older the GPU: on an A100 80GB, moving from the 90th-percentile provider to the 10th cuts the hourly rate by about 72% (1 - $1.00 / $3.52 = 0.72), while on a B200 the binding question is whether anyone has stock. Our map of the cheapest cloud GPUs explains where the low-end offers come from and what they trade away.

Three prices for the same GPU-hour

Floor, on-demand median outside the hyperscalers, and hyperscaler median, daily fixing of Oct 11, 2026

| Gpu | Floor | On-demand median | Hyperscaler median |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| A100 80GB | $0.87 | $1.93 | $3.55 |
| H100 SXM | $1.68 | $3.95 | $6.88 |
| H200 | $2.69 | $4.54 | $10.00 |
| B200 | $3.69 | $7.13 | $14.00 |
| B300 | $4.89 | $9.51 | $16.40 |

Source: FastGPU daily fixings, Oct 11, 2026, CC BY 4.0

The basis is the gap between the price a contract follows and the price you pay. It matters now because CME Group's exchange NYMEX has asked the CFTC to approve two cash-settled futures contracts on GPU rental prices, one for the H100 and one for the B200, settling on the monthly average of Silicon Data's H100 rental index and its B200 counterpart - NYMEX Submission No. 26-370. Each contract covers 730 GPU-hours, one GPU for an average month. FastGPU does not reproduce the index values, which belong to their publisher; its own fixings show how far apart the prices a buyer might actually pay sit. In the October 11 fixing, the H100 SXM's on-demand median outside the hyperscalers was $2.27 above the floor and the hyperscaler median another $2.93 above that. For the B200 the two gaps were $3.44 and $6.87. A hyperscaler customer paying $6.88 for an H100 SXM is paying about four times the $1.68 floor ($6.88 / $1.68 = 4.1).

...

The GPU clouds that file annual reports write their equipment off over 4 to 6 years, and the length of that schedule decides how fast the cost of a GPU reaches the income statement. CoreWeave uses 6 years for its data-center computing equipment. Nebius wrote that its GPUs "are currently depreciated over four years" - Nebius Form 20-F - and has since extended servers and network equipment to 5 years from 2026. IREN uses 5 years for its HPC hardware. The hyperscalers report one life for all servers, from 5 years at Amazon for a subset to 6 years at Alphabet; the depreciation page quotes each filing word for word.

The page sets those schedules against Epoch AI's estimate of what each chip cost its buyer and the GPU's median posted on-demand price outside the hyperscalers. Book cost per GPU-hour is the chip cost spread evenly over the useful life (a year is 8,760 hours). Payback is the chip cost divided by what the median rent earns in a month of 730 hours. For the H100 SXM, Epoch's chip estimate is $25,000; spread over CoreWeave's schedule that is $0.48 per GPU-hour, over Nebius's four years $0.71. The median rent of $3.95/hr across 20 providers is about eight times the six-year book cost ($3.95 / $0.48 = 8.2).

| GPU | Chip cost (Epoch AI estimate) | Median rent | Book cost per GPU-hour, 6-year life | Months to pay back, rented every hour |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| A100 80GB | $12,000 | $1.93/hr | $0.23 | 8.5 |
| H100 SXM | $25,000 | $3.95/hr | $0.48 | 8.7 |
| MI300X | $12,500 | $2.49/hr | $0.24 | 6.9 |
| H200 | $25,000 | $4.54/hr | $0.48 | 7.5 |
| B200 | $37,000 | $7.13/hr | $0.70 | 7.1 |
| MI355X | $27,500 | $4.42/hr | $0.52 | 8.5 |
| B300 | $43,000 | $9.51/hr | $0.82 | 6.2 |

...

An hourly price is not a price per unit of work. The GPU performance per rented dollar page takes each GPU's best result in MLPerf® Inference v6.1 (Closed division, Available category, datacenter, round published September 16, 2026), divides it by the GPUs in the submitted system, then by the GPU's live rental price. The per-GPU and per-dollar figures are FastGPU's derivations, not verified by MLCommons, and the benchmark is used only as a common yardstick for comparing GPUs.

...

All three figures are derived and unverified. The caveat is coverage: the MI355X median of $5.99/hr rests on only 3 providers, so its floor is one offer, not a market.

results.title: AWS Raises Nvidia GPU Reservation Prices 20% | TEXXR
highlights:
In 2014, Amazon Web Services cut S3 prices by up to 22%. It has since raised advance-reserved Nvidia GPU prices in EC2 Capacity Blocks by 20%, while leaving Trainium prices unchanged.

## Key takeaways

- AWS cut S3 prices by up to 22% in 2014 and EBS prices by up to 50% that year.
- AWS raised advance-reserved Nvidia GPU prices in EC2 Capacity Blocks by 20% while leaving Trainium prices unchanged.
- The Ornn Compute Price Index put Blackwell GPU rentals at $4.08 per hour in April, up 48% from $2.75 two months earlier.
- AWS said Project Rainier, built for Anthropic, uses more than 500,000 Trainium2 chips.
- Recursive Superintelligence signed a $410 million multiyear AWS compute agreement after raising $650 million in May.

...

AWS also cut EBS prices by up to 50% in 2014. Nine years later, S3 Express One Zone offered writes ten times faster and request costs 50% lower than standard S3. The latter is a request-price comparison, not a claim that every storage bill fell. Both moves show how AWS could pair lower prices for a defined unit with a more specialized service.

An Nvidia reservation has a constraint that a storage request does not: the customer needs the right machines available together at the appointed time. AWS cannot make an unavailable block useful by lowering the price of some other instance.

## A reservation insures the schedule, not the spot price

EC2 Capacity Blocks lets businesses rent AI compute in advance. The buyer commits to a block rather than assuming that equivalent capacity will be available later on demand. This is operational insurance against a delayed run, not a financial option that lets the buyer walk away if prices fall.

On-demand prices can move while a buyer holds an advance booking. In April, the Ornn Compute Price Index put a Blackwell GPU rental at $4.08 an hour, up 48% from $2.75 two months earlier. That index measures reported on-demand rentals, not AWS Capacity Blocks; it cannot establish AWS’s margin or the cause of its price change. It does show why a buyer with a fixed workload date might value certainty separately from an hourly discount.

...

### Which Nvidia GPU models and Capacity Blocks reservation lengths are affected by AWS’s 20% increase?

The piece does not specify the affected Nvidia models, block durations, prior prices, or effective date of the increase. It establishes only that advance-reserved Nvidia capacity rose 20% while Trainium pricing was unchanged.

...

## Reported cloud price and capacity signals

| Service or capacity | Reported change or scale | Time reference |
| --- | --- | --- |
| AWS S3 | Prices cut by up to 22% | 2014 |
| AWS EBS | Prices cut by up to 50% | 2014 |
| AWS EC2 Capacity Blocks for Nvidia GPUs | Advance-reservation prices raised 20% | Not specified |
| Blackwell GPU on-demand rentals | $4.08/hour, up 48% from $2.75/hour | April; comparison with two months earlier |

results.title: Why GPU Cloud Prices Keep Rising in 2026 (and How to Stay Ahead of the Next Hike) | OpenTencor AI
highlights:
All price figures in this guide are illustrative examples for education — never offers ... Market numbers attributed to third parties reflect reporting at the time of writing, and cloud prices change often. Before provisioning anything, check the provider's official pricing page. See our provider directory for where to find live rates.

...

If your GPU bills have been creeping up this year, it isn't your imagination. The most visible signal came from Nebius, which put through a blanket price increase across its GPU cloud services effective October 1, 2026, averaging roughly 20% across multiple chip models including the H100 and H200 — its second round of increases since May, according to EQS Newswire reporting on the announcement.

The more telling detail in that same reporting: some Nebius clients have reserved computing capacity as far ahead as 2028, and the company describes demand visibility stretching beyond 24 months. When customers are willing to book compute two years out at rising prices, the sellers hold the pricing power — and they know it.

...

The net effect: demand for GPU hours grows faster than anyone's datacenter buildout schedule, and price is the rationing mechanism.

...

| Market segment | Who they are | How they price |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Hyperscalers | AWS, Google Cloud, Azure | Premium, stable on-demand rates; best value via reserved/spot commitments |
| Neoclouds | CoreWeave, Nebius, Lambda, Crusoe | GPU-first, often reserved by the node; pricing power when capacity is pre-booked years out |
| Marketplaces | Vast.ai, RunPod community | Variable spot-like rates; often cheapest per GPU-hour, least predictable |
| Serverless inference | Together, Hyperbolic, Cerebrium | Per-token or per-second; shields you from GPU rental entirely for open-weight models |

...

1. Right-size the GPU. The most expensive mistake in the cloud is renting an H100 for a job a 4090 or L40 could do. Match the GPU to the model size — a 7B–13B model rarely needs a datacenter card. Our VRAM sizing guide shows how to pick the smallest card that fits.
2. Use spot and preemptible capacity. Interruptible instances typically cut 50–70% off on-demand rates. Batch jobs, fine-tuning with checkpoints, and offline inference pipelines are ideal candidates — anything where an interruption costs you minutes, not customers.
3. Commit when your usage is predictable. Reserved and committed-use pricing is the mirror image of the Nebius story: providers discount heavily for guaranteed revenue. If your workload is steady for months, buying your predictability back at a discount beats riding the on-demand market.
4. Move stable workloads to serverless inference. For serving open-weight models, per-token serverless endpoints remove you from the GPU-rental price cycle entirely — the provider absorbs the capacity risk. Compare the per-token math against your token volume before switching.
5. Shrink the compute per token. Quantization, smaller distilled models, speculative decoding, and batching reduce GPU-hours per unit of output — the one lever that works against every price hike, from every provider, simultaneously. Our cost-saving strategies guide walks through the full playbook.

results.title: a16z chart: GPU rental prices hold firm while token prices fall, a Jevons-style pattern | Dealroom News
highlights: Nathan LeClaire flagged an a16z Growth chart, compiled by Citadel Securities from Ornn, Silicon Data and Bloomberg data as of August 2026, that tracks the H100 GPU rental price against a token-price expenditure index. In late spring the two moved down together, but from July token prices kept falling, with the index dropping from roughly 1.6 to about 1.0, while the H100 rental price stayed at around $2.7 an hour. The chart is titled "Jevons: Compute Prices Rise As Token Prices Fall": cheaper tokens appear to be lifting demand for compute rather than easing it. Theo (t3.gg) quote-posted it with the comment "Called it".
